metadata.title: The relationship between inquiry-based teaching and students’ achievement. New evidence from a longitudinal PISA study in England

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for England (15/16-year-olds in Year 11) and applies the PISA complex survey design in estimation. The authors describe a stratified and clustered two-stage sample (schools sampled with probability proportional to size, then pupils randomly selected within schools) and follow the PISA recommendation to use Balanced-Repeated-Replication (BRR) weights to account for both stratification and clustering when estimating standard errors. They report that BRR weights were applied throughout the analyses, implying survey-weighted estimation rather than simple random-sample standard errors. The manuscript does not name a specific student weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but the use of BRR indicates weight-aware inference consistent with PISA’s resampling framework.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2015 England sample of 15/16-year-olds (Year 11) with science as the focus domain. The PISA sample was linked to England’s National Pupil Database (NPD) for 95% of the full sample to obtain GCSE science pillar scores and prior attainment (KS2). The analytic sample therefore consists of linked cases with available GCSE science pillar points and the covariates used in the preferred regression specification; the authors also state that imputation was used to account for small amounts of item non-response.

main_findings.target_variable: GCSE science achievement (pillar score) — disciplinary climate implementation proxy
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 5: when splitting by thirds of disciplinary climate (student-reported and school-average), inquiry quartile differences remain small and statistically insignificant; even in classrooms with good disciplinary climate, top vs bottom inquiry quartile difference is ~0.1 SD. Additional analysis (GCSE science achievement (pillar score)): OLS regression with inquiry-teaching quartiles (standardized GCSE outcome). Top vs bottom inquiry quartile: small positive in M2 (~0.1 SD increase); stable in M3; not statistically significant in preferred M4 (full controls). Additional analysis (GCSE science achievement (pillar score) — guidance moderation): Preferred Model 4: among pupils reporting high guidance, inquiry quartiles 3 and 4 show occasional small positive associations with effect sizes ~0.02 to 0.16; no relationship for low-guidance group; no significant effects for high inquiry with low guidance or high guidance with low inquiry. Additional analysis (GCSE science achievement (pillar score) — subgroup heterogeneity): Model 4 subgroup analyses by gender, ESCS group (low/average/high), and prior achievement: estimated effects are small and not statistically significant at the 5% level for all groups.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 England (Year 11) Science the study leveraged disciplinary climate as an implementation proxy alongside student and school context variables to predict GCSE science achievement (pillar score), finding that inquiry-based teaching shows no meaningful improvement even in science classrooms with good disciplinary climate (differences remain small, ~0.1 SD, and statistically insignificant). This indicates that implementation problems alone may not explain the overall null association, and that guidance and instructional design details may be more informative than discipline levels.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2015 science data for England (Year 11; N=5,194 pupils from 206 schools) linked to England’s National Pupil Database to obtain GCSE science pillar scores taken about six months after the PISA test. The primary outcome is GCSE science achievement, with PISA science scores used as a secondary outcome in robustness checks. The authors estimate OLS regression models with extensive controls for demographics, prior achievement (KS2 and PISA science), science course type, and additional student and school context; they apply PISA’s complex survey design using BRR weights and impute small item non-response. Across four model specifications, higher inquiry-teaching frequency shows at most a small (~0.1 SD) association that becomes non-significant once full controls are included. The paper reports no consistent positive effects across inquiry components, subgroups, or disciplinary-climate splits, with only tentative evidence that moderate inquiry combined with high teacher guidance may yield small gains. Limitations include reliance on observational associations (no causal identification) and the use of standardized GCSE/PISA measures that may not capture all inquiry-relevant skills.
